episodes.subject: coa
episodes.title: Computer foundations
episodes.description: Understand how computers execute a program.

turns.speaker: maya
turns.text: Hi, I'm Maya. Leo's with me, and today's section is called Computer foundations.

turns.speaker: leo
turns.text: Meet the machine behind the magic.

turns.speaker: maya
turns.text: Here's what we're working toward: understand how computers execute a program.

turns.speaker: leo
turns.text: We'll begin with architecture vs organization and work our way to RAM and ROM.

turns.speaker: leo
turns.text: Let's start with architecture vs organization. What do we need to know?

turns.speaker: maya
turns.text: A computer follows small encoded instructions. Architecture defines their meaning; organization is the hardware that carries them out.

turns.speaker: leo
turns.text: Bit means one binary digit, 0 or 1. Eight bits make a byte.

turns.speaker: leo
turns.text: In a toy 8-bit instruction 10 001101, the format might reserve the first two bits for an operation and the other six for an operand.

turns.speaker: maya
turns.text: The bit pattern has no instruction meaning until the format and operation codes are defined.

turns.speaker: leo
turns.text: That takes us to stored-program architecture. Where does it fit?

turns.speaker: maya
turns.text: A program combines instructions to solve a larger task. In a stored-program computer, memory holds the instructions as well as the data used during execution.

turns.speaker: leo
turns.text: CPU means central processing unit, the hardware that executes instructions.

turns.speaker: leo
turns.text: Starting from 5, how many ADD 5 operations reach 20?

turns.speaker: maya
turns.text: The accumulator visits 10, 15, then 20. That takes three additions.

turns.speaker: maya
turns.text: So we'd choose 3.

turns.speaker: maya
turns.text: Storage keeps a program for later use. Loading places its instructions and data in main memory, where the CPU can access them.

turns.speaker: leo
turns.text: Main memory (RAM) holds active instructions and data.

turns.speaker: leo
turns.text: When you launch a saved application, the operating system loads it into RAM. The CPU fetches an instruction, interprets it and performs its action.

turns.speaker: maya
turns.text: A process is the running program together with its execution state.

turns.speaker: maya
turns.text: Input and output are named relative to the computer. A device can serve both roles at different times.

turns.speaker: leo
turns.text: Input means information entering the computer.

turns.speaker: leo
turns.text: A scanner sends a scanned image into the computer. It is acting as…

turns.speaker: maya
turns.text: The information travels from the external source into the computer.

turns.speaker: maya
turns.text: We end up with An input device.

turns.speaker: leo
turns.text: How would you explain RAM and ROM to someone meeting it for the first time?

turns.speaker: maya
turns.text: Different storage technologies serve different purposes. Volatile memory needs power to keep its contents; nonvolatile storage retains information without power.

turns.speaker: leo
turns.text: RAM means working memory used while programs run.

turns.speaker: leo
turns.text: An unsaved edit may exist only in RAM and disappear after power loss. A saved copy on an SSD persists.

turns.speaker: maya
turns.text: Startup firmware runs before the operating system is loaded into RAM.

turns.speaker: leo
turns.text: Before we leave computer foundations, let's connect the pieces.

turns.speaker: maya
turns.text: A computer follows small encoded instructions. Architecture defines their meaning; organization is the hardware that carries them out.

turns.speaker: leo
turns.text: Different storage technologies serve different purposes. Volatile memory needs power to keep its contents; nonvolatile storage retains information without power.

turns.speaker: maya
turns.text: Try explaining RAM and ROM in your own words. If you get stuck, that chapter is a good place to listen again.

episodes.subject: coa
episodes.title: Memory & the system bus
episodes.description: Solve addressability, endianness, expansion, and interleaving problems.

turns.speaker: maya
turns.text: Welcome back. Maya here, with Leo. We've reached the section called Memory & the system bus.

turns.speaker: leo
turns.text: Give every byte a place to call home.

turns.speaker: maya
turns.text: Here's what we're working toward: solve addressability, endianness, expansion, and interleaving problems.

turns.speaker: leo
turns.text: We'll begin with main memory and addressability and work our way to memory interleaving GATE practice.

turns.speaker: leo
turns.text: That takes us to main memory and addressability. Where does it fit?

turns.speaker: maya
turns.text: Memory is divided into addressable cells. The address chooses a cell, and the cell width says how many bits that one address stores.

turns.speaker: leo
turns.text: Address means a number identifying a memory location.

turns.speaker: leo
turns.text: A chip with 10 address bits has 1,024 cells. If each cell contains 8 bits, its capacity is 1,024 × 8 bits = 1,024 bytes.

turns.speaker: maya
turns.text: Doubling cell width doubles capacity without adding addresses.

turns.speaker: leo
turns.text: There's another piece to this: byte ordering and endianness.

turns.speaker: maya
turns.text: A value wider than one byte occupies several consecutive byte addresses. Endianness determines which of its bytes is stored first.

turns.speaker: leo
turns.text: Hexadecimal means base 16; digits 0–9 and A–F. Two hex digits encode one byte.

turns.speaker: leo
turns.text: Does endianness change the numeric value of a correctly read integer?

turns.speaker: maya
turns.text: A reader using the matching byte-order convention reconstructs the same integer.

turns.speaker: maya
turns.text: So we'd choose No.

turns.speaker: maya
turns.text: Solve byte-order problems by drawing addresses first and placing bytes second. A narrow read uses only the requested bytes. A wider read may include neighboring objects, so explicitly identify the bytes involved before reconstructing the number.

turns.speaker: leo
turns.text: Most significant byte means the byte with the greatest positional weight.

turns.speaker: leo
turns.text: Store 0x1234 at byte addresses 100 and 101. Big endian places 0x12 at 100 and 0x34 at 101.

turns.speaker: maya
turns.text: Little endian places 0x34 at 100 and 0x12 at 101. The value is the same; only the byte arrangement changes.

turns.speaker: leo
turns.text: Byte order changes storage layout, not the numeric value.

turns.speaker: maya
turns.text: A memory transaction needs a location, a transferred value and an instruction to read or write. Bus signals carry these different kinds of information.

turns.speaker: leo
turns.text: Address bus selects a location.

turns.speaker: leo
turns.text: For a memory read, the data moves…

turns.speaker: maya
turns.text: A read returns the contents of the selected memory location to the processor.

turns.speaker: maya
turns.text: We end up with Memory to CPU.

turns.speaker: maya
turns.text: An address is not its stored value.

turns.speaker: leo
turns.text: I want to unpack memory interfacing and expansion next.

turns.speaker: maya
turns.text: To build a larger memory from small chips, decide whether you need more bits per address, more addresses, or both.

turns.speaker: leo
turns.text: Width expansion means chips operate in parallel at the same address.

turns.speaker: leo
turns.text: Two 1K × 4-bit chips sharing addresses can provide 1K × 8 bits.

turns.speaker: maya
turns.text: Two 1K × 8-bit banks can provide 2K × 8 bits, with an additional address bit choosing the bank.

turns.speaker: maya
turns.text: Interleaving spreads accesses among independently usable memory banks. Low-order interleaving uses the low address bits to choose the bank.

turns.speaker: leo
turns.text: Bank means one independently selected part of a memory.

turns.speaker: leo
turns.text: Four low-order-interleaved banks: which bank gets address 13?

turns.speaker: maya
turns.text: 13 mod 4 = 1. Here addresses are word addresses and banks are numbered 0 through 3.

turns.speaker: leo
turns.text: Before we leave memory & the system bus, let's connect the pieces.

turns.speaker: maya
turns.text: Memory is divided into addressable cells. The address chooses a cell, and the cell width says how many bits that one address stores.

turns.speaker: leo
turns.text: Interleaving spreads accesses among independently usable memory banks. Low-order interleaving uses the low address bits to choose the bank.

turns.speaker: maya
turns.text: When you try a problem on memory interleaving GATE practice, talk through why each step works. That's a useful check on what has clicked.

episodes.subject: coa
episodes.title: Instruction sets, opcodes and assembly
episodes.description: Trace registers, flags, instruction formats, opcodes, and branches.

turns.speaker: maya
turns.text: I'm Maya, and this is CSQuest Audio. Today, Leo and I are taking on Instruction sets, opcodes and assembly.

turns.speaker: leo
turns.text: Tiny instructions. Incredible possibilities.

turns.speaker: maya
turns.text: Here's what we're working toward: trace registers, flags, instruction formats, opcodes, and branches.

turns.speaker: leo
turns.text: We'll begin with registers and status flags and work our way to machine instruction GATE practice.

turns.speaker: leo
turns.text: There's another piece to this: registers and status flags.

turns.speaker: maya
turns.text: Registers are small storage locations inside the CPU. Flags describe properties of an arithmetic result, but their meaning depends on how the bits are interpreted.

turns.speaker: leo
turns.text: Unsigned n-bit integer means a value from 0 to 2^n − 1.

turns.speaker: leo
turns.text: In four bits, 0111 + 0001 produces 1000. Unsigned, that is 7 + 1 = 8 and fits.

turns.speaker: maya
turns.text: Signed, the result 8 is outside −8 to 7, so signed overflow occurs even without a final carry.

turns.speaker: leo
turns.text: Fetching an instruction is different from executing it.

turns.speaker: leo
turns.text: An effective address can differ from the operand value.

turns.speaker: leo
turns.text: Let's spend a moment on instruction set architecture.

turns.speaker: maya
turns.text: An instruction set architecture (ISA) specifies software-visible instructions, registers and behavior. Different CPU designs can implement that same contract.

turns.speaker: leo
turns.text: Register means fast storage inside a processor.

turns.speaker: leo
turns.text: Which belongs to the ISA?

turns.speaker: maya
turns.text: An instruction set defines what machine instructions do and how they are represented.

turns.speaker: maya
turns.text: So we'd choose Available instructions and their behavior.

turns.speaker: maya
turns.text: The introductory RISC/CISC comparison describes design tendencies. Classical RISC emphasizes simple instructions and register operations with explicit loads/stores. Classical CISC permits richer operations and addressing. Modern implementations can mix these ideas.

turns.speaker: leo
turns.text: Load/store means copy between memory and registers.

turns.speaker: leo
turns.text: A load/store design might load two memory values into registers, add the registers, then store the result. A richer instruction design may combine some of these operations.

turns.speaker: maya
turns.text: Both still need hardware that moves data and computes.

turns.speaker: maya
turns.text: An instruction format is a fixed budget of bits. Each field needs enough bit patterns to distinguish the operations, registers or addresses it represents.

turns.speaker: leo
turns.text: k-bit field means at most 2^k distinct patterns.

turns.speaker: leo
turns.text: 16-bit instruction: two 4-bit register fields. Remaining opcode bits?

turns.speaker: maya
turns.text: 16 - 4 - 4 = 8 bits remain for the opcode.

turns.speaker: leo
turns.text: Now for expanding opcode technique. What's the key distinction?

turns.speaker: maya
turns.text: An expanding opcode uses more opcode bits when fewer operand bits are needed. Reserve short opcode prefixes before allocating longer ones. A short opcode cannot also be the prefix of a longer opcode in a prefix-decoded format.

turns.speaker: leo
turns.text: Opcode means the operation-identifying part of an instruction.

turns.speaker: leo
turns.text: A 16-bit instruction with two register fields naming 8 registers needs 3 bits per field, leaving 10 bits for other fields.

turns.speaker: maya
turns.text: If short opcode 10 is reserved, a longer opcode starting with 10 would be ambiguous in a prefix-decoded format.

turns.speaker: maya
turns.text: Encoding problems are bit-budget and prefix-allocation problems. State how many registers or addresses each operand field represents. Count consumed prefixes at each format length before allocating the next format.

turns.speaker: leo
turns.text: Prefix means the starting bits of a code; prefix decoding must distinguish short and long opcodes.

turns.speaker: leo
turns.text: 16-bit instruction; two 4-bit operands. Root opcode width?

turns.speaker: maya
turns.text: The two operand fields consume eight bits, leaving eight root opcode bits.

turns.speaker: maya
turns.text: So we'd choose 8.

turns.speaker: maya
turns.text: The arithmetic logic unit (ALU) performs calculations and bitwise operations. For a fixed-width result, keep only the bits that fit and interpret them using the specified signedness.

turns.speaker: leo
turns.text: Shift means move all bits left or right; the fill rule must be specified.

turns.speaker: leo
turns.text: For 1010 and 1100, bitwise AND gives 1000, OR gives 1110 and XOR gives 0110.

turns.speaker: maya
turns.text: These operations compare corresponding bit positions, not the decimal values of the entire words.

turns.speaker: leo
turns.text: That takes us to branch instructions. Where does it fit?

turns.speaker: maya
turns.text: The program counter (PC) records an instruction address. A branch chooses a different next address, sometimes only when a condition is true.

turns.speaker: leo
turns.text: Branch target means the address execution jumps to.

turns.speaker: leo
turns.text: A taken branch directly changes…

turns.speaker: maya
turns.text: The program counter determines which instruction is fetched next.

turns.speaker: maya
turns.text: Trace machine programs one instruction at a time. Keep register values, flags, and PC in separate columns. Apply the stated operand width, addressing convention, and branch base; never mix a value with its address.

turns.speaker: leo
turns.text: Displacement means a signed distance from a specified base address.

turns.speaker: leo
turns.text: If a branch uses the next instruction at byte address 104 as its base and has displacement −8 bytes, the target is 96.

turns.speaker: maya
turns.text: If the displacement were −8 four-byte words, the target would instead be 104 − 32 = 72.

turns.speaker: leo
turns.text: An address is not its stored value.

turns.speaker: leo
turns.text: Byte order changes storage layout, not the numeric value.

turns.speaker: leo
turns.text: Before we leave instruction sets, opcodes and assembly, let's connect the pieces.

turns.speaker: maya
turns.text: Registers are small storage locations inside the CPU. Flags describe properties of an arithmetic result, but their meaning depends on how the bits are interpreted.

turns.speaker: leo
turns.text: Trace machine programs one instruction at a time. Keep register values, flags, and PC in separate columns. Apply the stated operand width, addressing convention, and branch base; never mix a value with its address.

turns.speaker: maya
turns.text: Take a small example of registers and status flags and work it out before looking at the explanation. Then compare your reasoning.

episodes.subject: coa
episodes.title: CPU execution and addressing modes
episodes.description: Trace execution and calculate effective addresses.

turns.speaker: maya
turns.text: Maya and Leo here. Our section today is CPU execution and addressing modes.

turns.speaker: leo
turns.text: Follow an instruction, one step at a time.

turns.speaker: maya
turns.text: Here's what we're working toward: trace execution and calculate effective addresses.

turns.speaker: leo
turns.text: We'll begin with instruction execution cycle and work our way to addressing modes III.

turns.speaker: leo
turns.text: Let's spend a moment on instruction execution cycle.

turns.speaker: maya
turns.text: Fetch, decode and execute describe how a CPU obtains an instruction and performs its operation. Register transfers show where each value goes.

turns.speaker: leo
turns.text: PC means program counter, identifying the next instruction location.

turns.speaker: leo
turns.text: In a simplified fetch, copy PC to MAR, read memory at that address into MDR, then copy the fetched instruction into IR.

turns.speaker: maya
turns.text: Updating PC prepares for the next fetch; a later branch may change it again.

turns.speaker: leo
turns.text: Fetching an instruction is different from executing it.

turns.speaker: leo
turns.text: An effective address can differ from the operand value.

turns.speaker: leo
turns.text: How would you explain addressing modes I to someone meeting it for the first time?

turns.speaker: maya
turns.text: An addressing mode says where an instruction gets its data. A value stored in a register may be the operand itself or an address pointing to the operand.

turns.speaker: leo
turns.text: Immediate means the instruction contains the value itself.

turns.speaker: leo
turns.text: Immediate operand #42: operand value?

turns.speaker: maya
turns.text: The number 42 is carried directly in the instruction, so no data-memory lookup is needed.

turns.speaker: maya
turns.text: Displacement-based modes combine a register value with an instruction field. Base-plus-displacement, indexed, and PC-relative examples all require clear units. Autoincrement and autodecrement also update their address register by the operand size.

turns.speaker: leo
turns.text: Effective address (EA) means the final memory location to access.

turns.speaker: leo
turns.text: If R holds 200 and memory[200] holds 9, register addressing uses 200 while register-indirect addressing reads 9.

turns.speaker: maya
turns.text: For base-plus-offset addressing with base 200 and offset 12 bytes, EA is byte address 212.

turns.speaker: leo
turns.text: An address is not its stored value.

turns.speaker: leo
turns.text: Byte order changes storage layout, not the numeric value.

turns.speaker: maya
turns.text: To compare addressing modes, trace the pointer calculation and count memory transactions. State whether instruction fetch is included. A register access is not a data-memory read, while memory indirection adds a pointer read.

turns.speaker: leo
turns.text: Indirect means follow a pointer to find the operand; a pointer read is a separate memory transaction.

turns.speaker: leo
turns.text: Direct memory operand: reads including one instruction fetch?

turns.speaker: maya
turns.text: One instruction read plus one operand read equals two reads under the stated toy model.

turns.speaker: maya
turns.text: We end up with 2.

turns.speaker: leo
turns.text: Before we leave CPU execution and addressing modes, let's connect the pieces.

turns.speaker: maya
turns.text: Fetch, decode and execute describe how a CPU obtains an instruction and performs its operation. Register transfers show where each value goes.

turns.speaker: leo
turns.text: To compare addressing modes, trace the pointer calculation and count memory transactions. State whether instruction fetch is included. A register access is not a data-memory read, while memory indirection adds a pointer read.

turns.speaker: maya
turns.text: You can pause here and try the CPU execution and addressing modes activities. Pick one idea and see whether you can explain it without the notes.

episodes.subject: coa
episodes.title: Cache mapping and replacement policies
episodes.description: Map addresses, trace hits and misses, and compare write policies.

turns.speaker: maya
turns.text: Hi, it's Maya. I've got Leo with me for Cache mapping and replacement policies.

turns.speaker: leo
turns.text: Make every memory access count.

turns.speaker: maya
turns.text: Here's what we're working toward: map addresses, trace hits and misses, and compare write policies.

turns.speaker: leo
turns.text: We'll begin with direct-mapped cache and work our way to write-back and write-through.

turns.speaker: leo
turns.text: How would you explain direct-mapped cache to someone meeting it for the first time?

turns.speaker: maya
turns.text: A cache keeps copies of memory blocks close to the CPU. A direct-mapped cache allows each block in exactly one line, so colliding blocks can replace each other.

turns.speaker: leo
turns.text: Block means the group of adjacent bytes transferred together.

turns.speaker: leo
turns.text: With 4-byte blocks and four cache lines, byte address 26 belongs to block floor(26/4)=6. Its line is 6 mod 4=2, tag is floor(6/4)=1, and byte offset is 26 mod 4=2.

turns.speaker: maya
turns.text: Check the line’s valid bit and tag before declaring a hit.

turns.speaker: leo
turns.text: A line index alone does not prove a hit; the entry must be valid and its tag must match.

turns.speaker: leo
turns.text: I want to unpack direct-mapped cache practice next.

turns.speaker: maya
turns.text: Trace a direct cache using memory block numbers, not raw byte addresses. Start with invalid lines, map each block, compare its tag, and update the line on a miss. Repeated accesses only hit if no conflicting block replaced the old one.

turns.speaker: leo
turns.text: Index selects a cache line. Tag: identifies which memory block currently occupies it.

turns.speaker: leo
turns.text: Cold direct cache: 4 lines. Blocks 0,1,0,4,0. Miss count?

turns.speaker: maya
turns.text: Miss on 0 and 1; hit on 0; block 4 replaces block 0; final 0 misses again.

turns.speaker: maya
turns.text: A set-associative cache maps a block to one set but allows it in any way within that set. A full set needs a replacement decision when a new block arrives.

turns.speaker: leo
turns.text: Way means one possible block slot within a set.

turns.speaker: leo
turns.text: A two-way set contains A then B. Reading A again makes B least recently used, so LRU replaces B on the next miss.

turns.speaker: maya
turns.text: FIFO still replaces A because it was inserted first.

turns.speaker: maya
turns.text: Replacement policies choose a victim within the mapped set. LRU tracks the most recent use and updates on hits. FIFO tracks insertion order and ignores hits for ordering. Different policies can therefore produce different traces.

turns.speaker: leo
turns.text: LRU means replace the least recently used block; hits update recency.

turns.speaker: leo
turns.text: For LRU, a cache hit…

turns.speaker: maya
turns.text: A successful access refreshes recency and can change which block will be evicted next.

turns.speaker: maya
turns.text: We end up with Makes the block most recently used.

turns.speaker: leo
turns.text: Let's start with loops, arrays, and cache. What do we need to know?

turns.speaker: maya
turns.text: Array layout determines the sequence of memory blocks a loop touches. Consecutive elements often share a block; revisiting a block helps only while it remains cached.

turns.speaker: leo
turns.text: Element size means bytes occupied by one array entry.

turns.speaker: leo
turns.text: A 3-column row-major matrix of 4-byte elements starts at address 100. Element [1][2], with zero-based indices, is at 100 + (1×3+2)×4 = 120.

turns.speaker: maya
turns.text: Moving down one row at a fixed column jumps 12 bytes.

turns.speaker: leo
turns.text: Byte order changes storage layout, not the numeric value.

turns.speaker: maya
turns.text: Traversal order matters for row-major matrices. A row groups adjacent elements; a column jumps by the row stride. Translate the loop into a block sequence before counting hits, and state whether data can survive until reuse.

turns.speaker: leo
turns.text: Row-major means all elements of a row are adjacent before the next row.

turns.speaker: leo
turns.text: Row-major 4×4 matrix, 4-byte elements. Row size in bytes?

turns.speaker: maya
turns.text: Four elements per row × four bytes each = sixteen bytes per row.

turns.speaker: maya
turns.text: So we'd choose 16.

turns.speaker: maya
turns.text: Average memory access time accounts for both common fast hits and less common slow misses. First decide whether a miss cost includes the cache lookup.

turns.speaker: leo
turns.text: Hit rate means fraction of accesses found in cache. Miss rate = 1 − hit rate.

turns.speaker: leo
turns.text: A cache takes 2 ns; 10% of accesses miss and incur an extra 40 ns. AMAT = 2 + 0.10×40 = 6 ns.

turns.speaker: maya
turns.text: Do not add the lookup twice if the problem instead gives a total miss time.

turns.speaker: leo
turns.text: Let's spend a moment on write-back and write-through.

turns.speaker: maya
turns.text: A write policy decides when changes reach lower memory. The allocation policy separately decides whether a missed store brings a block into cache.

turns.speaker: leo
turns.text: Write-through means forward each store to the lower level.

turns.speaker: leo
turns.text: A clean block eviction under write-back needs a data write-back?

turns.speaker: maya
turns.text: Clean data already agrees with the lower level, so eviction requires no dirty-data write.

turns.speaker: leo
turns.text: Before we leave cache mapping and replacement policies, let's connect the pieces.

turns.speaker: maya
turns.text: A cache keeps copies of memory blocks close to the CPU. A direct-mapped cache allows each block in exactly one line, so colliding blocks can replace each other.

turns.speaker: leo
turns.text: A write policy decides when changes reach lower memory. The allocation policy separately decides whether a missed store brings a block into cache.

turns.speaker: maya
turns.text: A useful next step is to revisit write-back and write-through with an example of your own. Keep it small enough to check by hand.

episodes.subject: coa
episodes.title: Fixed-point and floating-point representation
episodes.description: Encode fixed and floating point values and solve representation questions.

turns.speaker: maya
turns.text: Welcome to CSQuest Audio. I'm Maya, here with Leo. This section is called Fixed-point and floating-point representation.

turns.speaker: leo
turns.text: Small bits. Very big numbers.

turns.speaker: maya
turns.text: Here's what we're working toward: encode fixed and floating point values and solve representation questions.

turns.speaker: leo
turns.text: We'll begin with fixed-point representation and work our way to floating-point GATE practice.

turns.speaker: leo
turns.text: I want to unpack fixed-point representation next.

turns.speaker: maya
turns.text: A fixed-point format reserves a known number of fractional bits. Decode the stored signed or unsigned integer, then divide by the scale factor.

turns.speaker: leo
turns.text: Two’s complement means a leading 1 in an n-bit signed integer contributes −2^(n−1).

turns.speaker: leo
turns.text: With 8 signed bits and four fractional bits, 00011000 is integer 24 and means 24/16 = 1.5. The pattern 11101000 is integer −24 and means −1.5.

turns.speaker: maya
turns.text: The implied binary point is not stored as an extra bit.

turns.speaker: leo
turns.text: Unsigned carry and signed overflow differ.

turns.speaker: leo
turns.text: Now for floating-point representation. What's the key distinction?

turns.speaker: maya
turns.text: Floating point stores a value using a sign, a power-of-two exponent and significant binary digits. Not every real value has an exact finite encoding.

turns.speaker: leo
turns.text: Binary32 means one sign bit, eight exponent bits and 23 fraction bits.

turns.speaker: leo
turns.text: Binary32 exponent bias?

turns.speaker: maya
turns.text: Normal exponent fields use bias 127 to encode negative and positive exponents.

turns.speaker: maya
turns.text: Representation problems require identifying normal versus special values before applying a formula. Binary32 has finite precision, so not every real number is exact. Practice both encoding known binary fractions and recognizing reserved exponent patterns.

turns.speaker: leo
turns.text: Normal value means (−1)^sign × (1.fraction) × 2^(stored exponent−127).

turns.speaker: leo
turns.text: The binary value 101.1 equals decimal 5.5 and normalizes to 1.011 × 2^2. For binary32 its sign is 0, stored exponent is 2+127=129, and fraction begins 011 followed by zeros.

turns.speaker: maya
turns.text: The leading 1 is implicit for normal values.

turns.speaker: leo
turns.text: Floating-point rounding can lose information.

turns.speaker: leo
turns.text: Before we leave fixed-point and floating-point representation, let's connect the pieces.

turns.speaker: maya
turns.text: A fixed-point format reserves a known number of fractional bits. Decode the stored signed or unsigned integer, then divide by the scale factor.
